summary: Georgian Bay light at Cape Croker: an electric light and fog alarm in 1902, a concrete tower in 1909, and its lens moved to a museum in 2009.

lens.where: Bruce County Museum and Cultural Centre, Southampton (on loan from the Coast Guard)

access.note: Cape Croker, part of the Chippewas of Nawash First Nation community (LighthouseFriends). Visitors should ask the First Nation first.

visit.note: Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Not open for tours; can be viewed and photographed (Visit Lions Head).

events.note: Light and fog alarm put in operation on the point on 5 July 1902 (1902 report). The record's 1898 date is unconfirmed; tourism pages give it.
Electric fog alarm, powered by a plant in the building. The plant failed to give satisfaction (1902 report).
Electric light changed to a fixed light with a short eclipse (LighthouseFriends).
Compressed-air fog siren replaced the electric fog horn (LighthouseFriends).
Separate fog alarm building with diaphone, in operation 20 July 1905 (1905 report).
Tug A Seaman of Toronto burned near Cape Croker; no casualties (1906 report).
Tug Esperanza of Toronto caught fire near Cape Croker; cause unknown; no casualties (1908 report).
Steamer J. H. Jones lost off Cape Croker, 22 November 1906, in a gale.
Small coal dock and concrete-lined well added (1908 report; LighthouseFriends dates the well to 1908).
Reinforced concrete octagonal tower built 1909 (1909 Chief Engineer report names W. C. Surtees superintending; LighthouseFriends gives the Forest City Paving contract).
Steam fog alarm plant replaced by an oil plant (LighthouseFriends).
Two-storey keeper's residence and fog alarm building demolished (LighthouseFriends).
Last keeper left; the lighthouse was left unmanned (LighthouseFriends; Visit Lions Head).
Coast Guard removed the third-order Fresnel lens because vandalism threatened the tower.
Lens placed on loan at the Bruce County Museum and Cultural Centre under a long-term lease.

wrecks.outcome: Steamer of Goderich, left Owen Sound in a heavy gale for Lion's Head; last seen off Cape Croker; lifeboats and wreckage ashore at Christian Island. Department: about twenty-two lost. Yale Expositor: 26 known lost.

Tug of Toronto, caught fire near Cape Croker. Cause unknown. No casualties.

corrections.why: The Canadian Coast Guard list gives the light at 44 57 21.3 N, 080 57 38.1 W, about 14 m from the record's OSM point. Proposed to use the Coast Guard position.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1902 report and the Coast Guard list put the light on a point south-east of Cape Croker, one and a half miles SE of the cape; LighthouseFriends places it on the northeast extremity of the cape. The story follows the 1902 report and the Coast Guard list and states the disagreement.

notes_for_editor: 1) First light: the record's 1898 (Rowlett) and the tourism pages' 1898 wooden light are not confirmed. The Marine corpus for this station starts with the 1902 report, which describes the light and alarm as put in operation on 5 July 1902 and mentions no earlier light. first_lit is set to 1902; if a primary 1898 record turns up, restore it. 2) Keeper names for 1903, 1906 and 1907 were matched by adjacency in OCR keeper lists ('Chapman, Richard' next to 'Cape Croker'); check scans 221 (1903 list), 172 (1906 list) and 142 (1907 list). Keepers after 1910 come only from LighthouseFriends. 3) Esperanza report OCR reads 'sajik' for 'sank'; the story does not rely on that word. 4) Fatality counts disagree: department 'about twenty-two' (1907 report) against the Yale Expositor's 26 'known to have been lost'; the story gives both and resolves nothing. The newspaper's account of who found the bodies is not repeated. 5) LighthouseFriends says the 1902 alarm was the first electric light and fog alarm in Canada; the 1902 report itself says a similar alarm was in use at Victoria Harbour, BC, so the claim is left out. 6) The lens photo caption is by a photographer tagged to the museum; no museum text was found. 7) Post-1960 keepers (Whetton, Rourke, Adams, Proulx) are named only in their public role, with no personal detail; the sunstroke and lightning anecdotes were left out. 8) The reserve's status is from tourism and museum sources; no Chippewas of Nawash visiting rule was found. 9) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1907 keeper-list page image (scan 142) was viewed and shows Chapman, Richard on the same row as Cape Croker Light and Fog Alarm (appointed 13 1902). The 1903 and 1906 keeper rows were matched on one OCR line (name and station together), not by column, and their page images were not viewed. The 1902 report (printed p. 60) supplies the August machinery failure and the $3,358.78 cost. The Neyaashiinigmiing and Unceded wording was removed: no cited source gives the reserve name (the Flickr caption, footnote 12, is the only one that says Unceded, and it is not used for the land). The location disagreement with LighthouseFriends is now stated in the story.
